explore_prose: Each row below is one BLIS replay run. The load axis is session-tree lanes, not in-flight requests: one lane drives a whole agent trajectory that fans out into many sub-requests, so a lane is worth far more concurrency than a single chat turn.

The interactivity floor is the default 50 tok/s per user (ITL p99 ≤ 20 ms). That is a chatbot floor, and it is worth saying plainly that it may be the wrong one for an agent: these requests carry 92,947 tokens of context and their p99 time-to-first-token is 10 s, so a user waits seconds before the first token regardless of how fast the stream then runs. It is kept because it discriminates sharply on this workload — the winner holds 106.3 tok/s/user at 64 lanes and collapses to 6.5 at 128

glossary.def: One live agent trajectory, not one request.
glossary.long: An AgentX lane replays a whole recorded coding session: a main turn, its sub-agent groups and their inner requests. One lane therefore puts many requests in flight, which is why the lane ladder is much shorter than a request-concurrency ramp.

glossary.def: tp × pcp × dp — derived, never declared.
glossary.long: A width of 1 shards no experts, so it neither saves memory nor costs collectives. This is why adding dp rescues a layout that failed at the same tp.

glossary.def: C* is the highest load meeting the floor; the recommendation is 0.8 × C*.
glossary.long: The reported figures are measured AT the usable load, not read off a nearby rung of the ladder, so the throughput quoted is the throughput at the load recommended.

glossary.def: About 118 input tokens per output token on this corpus.
glossary.long: Output tok/s per GPU is the ranking metric but a poor description of the machine's work here: most of each request is reading context, so a low output rate can coexist with very high total token throughput.

hero.html: The 12 highest-ranked of 19 valid expert-parallel and tensor-parallel layouts that fill 64 GPUs, probed up a session-lane ladder and refined one engine knob at a time — 203 runs, 12 candidate topologies, 20 refinement arms, 23 servable finalists, 13 shapes the simulator refused or that missed the floor.

This is a prefill-dominated workload: 92,947 input tokens per request against 791 output, about 118:1. Output tok/s per GPU reads low by chatbot standards because almost all the work is reading context — the winner is ingesting roughly 87,854 input tok/s.

8x TP8 + EP at 51 concurrent agent sessions (80% of the measured ceiling of 64). Expert parallelism is not optional here: no non-EP control produced a servable run (13 shape(s) refused or below the floor).

meta: AgentX MVP replay (393 recorded Claude Code trajectories)
recommendation_prose: 8x TP8 + EP at 51 concurrent agent sessions, on the h100 deployment flags in the table below. That is 747.6 output tok/s across 64 GPUs (11.7 per GPU) at 119.2 tok/s per user and ITL p99 8.4 ms.
Leave the engine knobs at their defaults. None of the refinements helped, and the routing profiles in particular cost capacity on this traffic.

These are simulator predictions over a recorded corpus, not a live cluster measurement. The corpus is pinned by sha256, so the traffic is reproducible; the pricing is the blis-latency-kernel cost model and should be spot-checked against real serving data before anyone sizes a cluster from it.

sections.caption_note: The winner's ceiling is 64 lanes. The recommendation sits at 51, measured directly rather than interpolated.
prose: Throughput climbs almost linearly with lanes and then falls off a cliff. 8x TP8 + EP holds 106.3 tok/s per user at 64 lanes, and at 128 lanes per-user rate collapses to 6.5 tok/s while ITL p99 jumps from 9.4 ms to 154 ms.
The cliff is why the recommendation is 51 lanes and not the ceiling: at the ceiling there is no headroom for a burst, and this workload's bursts are whole agent trajectories waking up at once.
sections.title: The operating curve, and where it stops

sections.caption_note: Only expert-parallel layouts appear: no control produced a servable run.
prose: The search runs every expert-parallel candidate beside its non-EP control, because the direction is meant to be measured rather than assumed. Here the comparison is not close: every one of the 5 non-EP controls failed outright, and all 23 finalists are expert-parallel.

The failures are memory, not throughput — “No available memory for the cache blocks”, or a per-rank fixed occupancy above the 79.2 GiB device. Sharding the experts is what makes a 256k-token context fit on this part at all. It is also why the narrow-TP shapes die even with EP on: the expert-parallel width is derived as tp × dp, so a width of 1 shards nothing.
sections.title: Expert parallelism is load-bearing, not an optimisation

sections.caption_note: Crosses are runs that missed the interactivity floor.
prose: Refinement moves one knob at a time off the winning topology, so any difference is attributable. Nothing improved on the defaults — these knobs constrain:

• 1 draft token: 6.1 tok/s/GPU, -47.9% — and it halves usable capacity, C* 64 → 32
  • queue-kv routing: 6.3 tok/s/GPU, -46.2% — and it halves usable capacity, C* 64 → 32
  • 3 draft tokens: 7.0 tok/s/GPU, -40.2% — and it halves usable capacity, C* 64 → 32
  • 5 draft tokens: 7.1 tok/s/GPU, -39.3% — and it halves usable capacity, C* 64 → 32
  • batch tokens 2,048: 10.4 tok/s/GPU, -11.1%
  • prefix-affinity routing: 11.5 tok/s/GPU, -1.7%
  • max seqs 64: 11.6 tok/s/GPU, -0.9%

The expensive one is 1 draft token at -47.9%. It is not a small scheduling inefficiency: it drops the servable ceiling from 64 lanes to 32. Drafting spends decode compute verifying tokens, which is compute the baseline spends on concurrency; at this depth the acceptance length does not pay for the draft, so the deployment buys per-session speed with sessions it cannot spare.
sections.title: The knobs that bind, and the one that really hurts

prose: This model ships its own drafter — the catalog graph declares a dspark speculator — so draft depth is a real deployment choice, not an exotic knob. Each depth is run against the no-drafting baseline on the winning topology:

• K=1: 6.1 tok/s/GPU, -47.9% against no drafting, acceptance length 1.81, ceiling 32 lanes
  • K=3: 7.0 tok/s/GPU, -40.2% against no drafting, acceptance length 2.9, ceiling 32 lanes
  • K=5: 7.1 tok/s/GPU, -39.3% against no drafting, acceptance length 3.51, ceiling 32 lanes

Read those percentages carefully: each arm is scored at its own usable load, and drafting moves that load. A depth whose ceiling drops is therefore scored at a lower session count than the baseline, which makes it look worse than it is at any load they share — the matched-load table below is the comparison that answers “should I turn this on”. Here the ceiling falls for K=1 (32 lanes against the baseline’s 64), K=3 (32 lanes against the baseline’s 64), K=5 (32 lanes against the baseline’s 64).

How to read the per-user rate on these rows. Under drafting the engine reports the inter-token latency of a verification step, and one step emits as many tokens as the target accepts. So the per-user token rate is the acceptance length times 1000/ITL p99, not 1000/ITL p99 — the naive reading understates a drafting configuration by the whole acceptance factor and can make the fastest configuration measured look like a floor violation. The rows above use the acceptance-scaled rate, and the explorer labels it as derived.

At matched load, drafting pays at some loads and not others (12 of 21 measured points improve on the baseline) — and it moves the interactivity cliff, so the two arms' own usable loads are not the same load. Output tok/s at each session count, with the change against no drafting:

The servable ceiling, however, falls: no drafting holds 64 lanes while K=1 at 32 lanes, K=3 at 32 lanes, K=5 at 32 lanes. Drafting spends decode compute verifying tokens, which is compute the baseline spends on concurrency — so the knob trades sessions for per-session speed. Set it from which of those you are short of: at a fixed session count below the drafting cliff it is close to free throughput, and above that cliff it costs you the sessions.

The acceptance lengths are measured, not assumed: they come from inferencex-golden-al (b200) in blis-registry, keyed by this model, drafter, depth, thinking mode and workload category. They were measured on another part and reused here; the profile set states that acceptance depends mostly on the model, drafter and workload rather than the chip, and asks that the reuse be recorded, so it is recorded on every row.
sections.title: Speculative decoding, and what it does to the interactivity number

prose: The same search at 32 and 64 GPUs on H100 makes the scaling explicit. Going from 32 to 64 GPUs multiplies fleet throughput by 1.04x (717.6 to 747.6 output tok/s) and the servable ceiling by 1.00x (64 to 64 lanes).

Per-GPU efficiency therefore falls from 22.4 to 11.7 tok/s/GPU (0.52x). Capacity scales but efficiency does not: the second half of the cluster is doing real work — the ceiling genuinely doubles — while each GPU does less of it. For a fixed interactivity target that is the honest trade, and it means the larger cluster is the right buy only if you need the extra 0 lanes of capacity, not if you are chasing tokens per GPU.
sections.title: What doubling the cluster buys

standfirst: A configuration search over 203 BLIS replay runs on 64× H100, driven by the recorded AgentX agentic traffic rather than a synthetic request shape. The winner is 8x TP8 + EP at 747.6 output tok/s (11.7 per GPU) while every user still reads at 119.2 tok/s.
title: Serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash to coding agents on 8 H100 nodes
